description:
Tashkent team working on "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data". We're building a climate advisor for Uzbek farmers, using NASA satellite data and physics-based models to guide irrigation and crop choices amid water shortages and the Aral Sea crisis.

Team: software engineers, a physics student, a motion designer and a video editor.
summary: Mission Architect is a free 3D game in which students design, manage and fly a real interplanetary mission. In first person, players walk around a spacecraft clean room, pick up real hardware (nuclear batteries, solar arrays, antennas, attitude control and 24 instruments modelled on NASA instruments) and install it, while live gauges show the effect on mass, power, delta-v, budget, data and science. They choose a launch window on a chart where every point is a trajectory computed from NASA/JPL planet positions, pick a rocket, and fly the spacecraft they built in 3D: launch, cruise, and a Mars landing, a Jupiter orbit insertion or a Pluto flyby. During the flight, Mission Control decisions based on real events, such as Juno's 2016 engine valve anomaly and New Horizons' hazard search, change the outcome. A report explains why the mission succeeded or failed and finds the one change that would have helped most. The physics is validated against Mars 2020 and New Horizons. The game answers the challenge by turning mission design, management and operations into one playable loop, and it teaches what NASA engineers really do: balance trade-offs and live with the consequences. A 4-minute training mission gets anyone started, in any browser, with no installation.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Architect turns the whole mission-design process into a game you play with your hands. There are three NASA-style missions: a Mars rover (beginner), a Jupiter orbiter (intermediate) and a Pluto flyby with a Jupiter gravity assist (advanced), each with three science goals and four difficulty levels.

1. Build: in a 3D clean room, players pick up and install power (solar or nuclear), batteries, backup computers, attitude control, a radiation vault, antennas, fuel, a landing system or science orbit, and 24 instruments. Every part changes mass, power, delta-v, cost, data and science, and the gauges preview the change before it is installed.

2. Plan: the launch-window chart ("porkchop plot") is computed live by a Lambert solver from NASA/JPL planet positions. Seven rockets, including ESA's Ariane 64 and JAXA's H3, have real payload-versus-energy curves.

3. Fly: after a GO/NO-GO poll, the launch plays on the pad, then the spacecraft flies in 3D to a Mars entry, parachute and sky-crane landing, a Jupiter orbit insertion burn, or the Pluto and Charon flyby. Random events from real missions (dust storms, safe modes, radiation, wheel failures) are survived only by the right design choices.

4. Decide: Mission Control stops the clock for real calls: a course correction, the landing site, dust-storm hibernation, Juno's engine valve anomaly, New Horizons' hazard search and planetary protection. Each call re-flies the mission with the same luck, so players see exactly what their decision changed.

5. Learn: the report explains why the mission worked or failed, re-flies the mission once for every single possible change to find the one that helps most, and compares the design with Perseverance, Juno, New Horizons, ESA's JUICE and Rosalind Franklin.

Team play: up to four players share one design. Each has a role (Flight Dynamics, Spacecraft Systems, Principal Investigator, Ground and Budget), their own stations, a personal goal that pulls against the others, and their own Mission Control calls.

HOW IT WORKS

The physics engine uses NASA/JPL planet ephemerides, Kepler propagation, a Lambert solver, patched-conic gravity assists, the rocket equation, orbit insertion delta-v, atmospheric entry speed, inverse-square solar power, RTG decay, a radio link budget calibrated to New Horizons and a radiation dose model. 21 automated tests check it: for example, Mars 2020 launch energy C3 is 14.4 in our engine against about 14.5 in reality, and New Horizons' speed at Pluto is 13.79 km/s against 13.8.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students learn why trade-offs matter instead of memorising facts. There is no single correct design, and every failure is explained and points to the station that fixes it. A 4-minute guided training mission, a colour-blind safe palette and a reduced-motion mode make it accessible, and a teacher guide is included. It is free, needs no account or installation, and runs in any modern browser (a Windows app is also available). The same trade-offs (mass, power, data, budget, risk) drive Earth-observing satellites that monitor climate, water and crops, so the skills carry over to problems on Earth.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz, players build the spacecraft by hand in first person and then watch the exact spacecraft they built fly. Decisions are taken from real NASA history, and the game re-flies the mission to show the consequence of every choice.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Three.js (3D), Vite, Vitest (tests), Electron (Windows app), GitHub Pages (hosting). All 3D models, textures and sounds are generated in code; the planet maps are real NASA images.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy (validated against real missions), playability for beginners (training mission, clear tasks), accessibility (colour-blind palette, reduced motion, runs on ordinary school laptops), and honesty about limits: rocket and cost numbers are rounded public values.
